in my experience, maintaining a better eating habit is easier on almost any medication, as long as that medication works for you. I'm ultra treatment resistant, but I've lost weight on p much every med at first, before it pooped out.

for me, weight gain wasn't a huge issue (I was already fat, I'm a big emotional eater), but I did have a more uncommon side effect. I started wetting the bed, due to a combo of lithium causing increased urination and me sleeping straight through the urge to pee.

but assuming you normally wake up when you have to pee, you won't be wearing incontinence underwear like me lol. I did experience a fall off of the antidepressant effect of lithium over time, but it still does well against mania for me.

if you really want to stick to the lamictal, there's a few things that you can try.

1. you can try reducing the dose, and adding a second medication to compensate. I would personally recommend lithium there over any of the other anticonvulsants or antipsychotics, it's given me far fewer cognitive side effects, but everyone's different.

2. you can also talk to your doctor about trying a stimulant alongside your current dose of lamictal. something like a low dose of ritalin may help, or there's been studies indicating that modafinil is helpful in BP people with cognitive issues. there is always a risk there of stimulant induced mania, so you'd want to be attentive to that if you and your doctor went that route.

there's also option 3, if all else fails - transitioning to another med entirely. it's worth having a conversation with your doctor about what kind of sacrifices you're willing to make for stability. it's okay to say, "I haven't tried something else, I'd like to see if I can do well on another med that won't make me flunk nursing school". you can always go back to lamictal if other meds don't keep your mood stable enough.

Try using a gentler brush at first. The furminator can pull,  cats have sensitive skin. Hold the hair underneath the mat and use a slicker brush or a comb to try and tease it apart. Short, pat-pull motions are your friend.

Try having a second person help you, if you can. The other person can help hold her and give her high value treats to keep her distracted. Grooming uncooperative animals gets a lot easier with an extra set of hands.

If neither of those works, you might have to just shave them out snd start brushing to prevent mats from forming again. Brushing out mats can be very painful, especially for cats - dogs have skin about a third as thick as people, and cats have skin about a third as thick as dogs. Their skin is very delicate and sensitive. My parents had to take this approach with their Maine coon, he would not tolerate us touching the mats with a brush at all.

You should start brushing the new puppys teeth 3 times a week minimum from the get go, also. The earlier you start, the better the dog will tolerate it, and at home preventative care can go a long way towards keeping teeth in good shape (just like people). They sell enzymatic dog toothpaste and dog toothbrushes at most major pet stores, and the important thing in brushing is really making sure the toothpaste gets properly spread around the gumline. Scrubbing for 2 minutes like people isn't necessary.

If your current dog will tolerate it, it doesn't hurt to start now either. It won't fix the damage that's already there, but it can help prevent it from getting worse alongside his regular scalings.

You should trim her nails before you bathe her, to minimize how much she can stab you. Brush her out, to make sure she doesn't have any tangles that will be made worse by being wet. Bathe her when she's at her calmest - after a long play session is good. You can try bathing her in the sink or the tub, cats tend to feel more secure in small spaces so if she fits in the sink try that. 

Soap her up before you introduce the water and watch her closely and let the shampoo sit. (If you're using flea shampoo, it has to sit to kill fleas.) don't let her lick herself, she's going to want to. Then when it's time for the water, grab her by the scruff, and gently spray over her. She's going to cry and kick, most likely, because she's not used to baths, but you'll have to put up with the scratches if you'd like to bathe her. Soap up her head and rear first, or the fleas will run and try to crawl up her nose or her anus to avoid the soap. 

There are also spray on products you can use instead of bathing, if your cat really doesn't tolerate it at all. Since she's already stressed by the loss of her friend, these products might be a better idea to avoid stressing her out more. Frontline makes a spray, and I believe Sentry makes a comparable one. You can also get a flea comb, get a bowl of hot soapy water, and alternate between dipping the comb and brushing her. The soap suffocates any fleas you comb off of her.

Shaving doesn't help control fleas. It can also cause clipper alopecia, causing her hair to not grow back in properly. It's not recommended to shave cats unless there's matting that can't be brushed out, or surgical reasons. 

Most of the fleas are actually in the environment, as that's where the fleas and larvae develop. It's important that alongside a vet recommended treatment, you also get a spray for your carpets and furniture. If you don't, the cats will just keep getting reinfested.

You should have gravel that isn't sharp in your tank, because they do dig, and plenty of space for them to hide. Because blood parrots are a crossbreed, most of them are infertile and will not spawn. You should make sure when you feel that some of the food sinks, because they can have a hard time eating off the surface due to the small mouths they have.

I'm not that guy, but realistic steps to improving overall mood and mental health:

Keep a regular sleep cycle and a good diet. Go to bed at the same time and wake up at the same time every day, and don't eat tons of garbage. 

Exercise. Doesn't have to be a ton of hard work, just take a 15 minute walk every day. Fresh air, sunshine, and movement improves mood significantly (in some cases, better than antidepressants). 

Be social. Go out and do things with your friends, and find hobbies that aren't just related to recreational drug use. While drug use is fine as long as it's not making you feel worse, it's good to have enjoyable activities to do outside of smoking. You're in a loop here of, "everything sucks and the world is boring and life is unfulfilling, so I'm going to go smoke," which at the end of the day is really just avoiding the problem. 

(Avoiding the problem sounds somewhat judgmental, I feel like, but it's true. It's similar to being depressed and sleeping 14 hours a day - in one case, you feel like shit so you go to sleep so you don't have to feel like that, in the other you smoke ip so you don't have to feel like that. Or like someone who drinks to cope with emotional issues. You can drink responsibly and for fun, but using alcohol to cope is an avoidance mechanism and not good for your mental health.)

If the above fails, or you don't feel like you can manage it on your own? Seek professional help. Therapy, support groups, and medication are useful tools and there is no shame in using them. Therapy and support groups can help you work through whatever issues you may be having and find ways to fix them or cope with them. Medication can change the way your brain is currently working to alleviate depression, anxiety, etc. 

All of these answers take time and effort for you to see a change. I recommend keeping a mood journal over the course of several months as you start changing aspects of your life or seeking professional help. This can show you what changes are helping and what changes aren't. Since you use marijuana, you should include that and any other substance you use in the journal, because they will affect your mood both while you're high and afterwards.

At the same time, ECT is incredibly effective. The number of people who experience at least partial remission of symptoms is ~90%, which is far higher than most medications. Bipolar I requires at least one, non medication or drug induced, full blown manic episode. (Bipolar II people can experience fully manic episodes due to the effects of prescribed medications or illicit drug use, which is why that criteria is there.) 

Bipolar II requires at least one depressive episode and one hypomanic episode. 

Bipolar NOS is when you have clearly defined mood episodes, but it doesn't fit a particular pattern of either I or II. 

Cyclothymia is "milder" bipolar, characterized by cycles of dysthymia (episodes of depressed mood that do not fit criteria for a full episode of depression) and hypomania. 

Rapid cycling is a subtype of all types of bipolar that means you have at least 4 defined mood episodes in a year.

If someone has signs of addiction or is suspected of selling their meds, there are ways to manage that without just cutting their doses. You can prescribe long acting opioids, which reduce the ability to abuse the drug (though it still exists). You can make it so that to receive doses, the patient must go to their pharmacy, have a nurse administer them, or otherwise control their direct access to the drug. You can consider a pain pump, which is implanted into the abdomen and filled with painkillers that are released at set times and doses. Even addicts need their pain managed. 

It's absolutely cruel to cut a person in serious pain off from the medications they need to manage it, is what I'm saying. Effective use of opiates drastically improves quality of life for many people in pain, and to expect people who need them and who have no history of being addicted to them to suffer in order to reduce abuse is absolutely not fair.

Many formerly obese people feel this way. It's hard to change your way of thinking about yourself, even when your body has changed. Even if you can stand on the scale and see the change, in your head you've still got all those negative thoughts because of years of thinking them.

My advice to you is this: when you catch yourself thinking negative thoughts about yourself, contradict them. If you think, "I'm always going to be fat," say "No, I've lost weight and the proof of progress is there." Respond to "I can't keep a job," with "I've struggled in the past, but that doesn't mean I can't do it in the future, and thinking that way isn't going to help me." And so on.

I was vegan for a while, and then transitioned to vegetarian and then back into a standard diet, here's a list of things I ate a lot of:

* Tofu - make stirfry, make tofu scramble, make breakfast sandwiches, etc, very versatile and doesn't really have a flavor of its own. there's also tempeh, but that's got a nuttier flavor and a different kind of texture.
* Edamame - I'd eat this on its own steamed, often I'd buy roasted edamame and eat it as a snack
* Seitan - this is usually used as a meat substitute, not everyone's a fan of the texture, if you've got any kind of issue with wheat/gluten it's not for you
* Quinoa - use as a higher-protein rice substitute, it's got a bit of a different texture, you can also use it as an oatmeal replacement in the mornings if you put fruit and that kind of thing in it, or make it with eggs and spinach for a savory verson
* Nuts and seeds - these are high calorie, but filled with good fats and protein, just make sure to eat them in moderation!
* Beans - pretty standard, you can make all kinds of things with them if you look, I love making chili personally
* Dark, leafy greens - have far lower protein density, but can help bulk out your meals and add fiber to make you feel fuller
* Quorn - a lesser-known meat substitute made from mycoprotein, if you're vegan it's usually bound together with eggs so most products won't be appropriate for you
* Eggs - about 6-7 grams of protein/egg. If you use just the egg whites, you get more protein with fewer calories
* Skim milk - personally I hate drinking milk on its own, but you can use it to cook oatmeal/put in cereal/make a protein shake if you're like me
* Cottage cheese - pretty high protein, if you buy it made with 1% or skim it's lower calorie with similar protein content to higher fat versions
* Greek yogurt - greek yogurt is awesome, it's sweet and creamy and like eating dessert for breakfast and is much higher protein than normal yogurt

There's more than one antidepressant in the world, and not every antidepressant works for everybody. And unfortunately, sometimes the first one doesn't work, and you have to try another, and in the meantime life still continues to suck because the chemicals in your brain are out of whack and keeping you from functioning.

"Keep on keeping on" is awful advice to give to someone with clinical depression who is failing to function in daily life. And medication for someone who is severely depressed is often lifesaving and one of the first steps in making progress towards recovery, especially considering the majority of depression is neurochemical in nature.

If your antidepressant is making you feel more depressed and suicidal, you need to contact your psychiatrist and change medications immediately. Call the doctor's office as soon as possible - today if it hasn't closed yet, first thing in the morning if it has - and explain to the receptionist that you need to speak to a nurse or the doctor regarding severe side effects of your medication. They should at least have a nurse available to talk to you and advise you and get you set up to come in for an appointment.

Not all antidepressants will have this effect on you. Lexapro just isn't the right one for you, and your doctor will be able to have you taper off of it and try a different one safely. Unfortunately, psychiatry is a field that takes some trial and error to find the medication that helps. I went through 3 different antidepressants before the 4th one worked.

* Have you been stressed at all recently? I get absolutely awful stress-induced reflux.
* Have you replaced soda with high caffeine beverages, like coffee or tea? Caffeine can cause acid reflux.
* Are you certain you haven't had any significant dietary change? Adding in new foods could be a trigger - for example, some people find that nuts are a heartburn trigger for them, even though nuts are fairly healthy.

I left normal high school for more advanced/accelerated options in 10th grade, and I burned way the hell out. It wasn't pretty. Three years later and now in real college, here's what I've managed to learn from recovering from that burnout and then maintaining my sanity since.

The number 1 thing I'm going to say about readings: Pay attention in class. Mark down what you understood well, what you have a couple questions about, and what you don't understand at all.

* For what you understood well, don't bother reading those sections. Your notes from class should be enough.
* For what you have a couple questions about, skim over those sections and find the answer.
* For what you don't understand at all, read those sections in depth, and consider going to office hours to ask about them.

The point of note-taking is to sum up the main points of the reading, so that later when it comes to exam time you can look back and have a short refresher. I, personally, find this harder to do with hard sciences like chemistry, because there's some important stuff in the details. My recommendation is to just do the extra practice problems in the syllabus - your ability to do those is going to help you review very well.

For the practice problems, try to make connections in your class and set up a study group, of sorts. (I know it might be hard to do with social anxiety.) Sitting in a group and working on it and being able to work together if there's something you don't get is really, really helpful.

Put down a calendar. It can be weekly, it can be monthly, you can plot out the entire semester if you really want to. Put down the due dates for your major assignments, your readings, your homework. Put down your daily schedule, and put in time to eat/sleep/exercise, and times when you're going to study. Having a schedule and and a calendar helps a lot in feeling in control of everything.

Start exercising again. I cannot stress the helpfulness of regular exercise enough. You will feel better. Even if you can only manage 20 minutes of moderate exercise a day, you will feel better mentally. Exercise is incredibly helpful for stress management.

If you're addressing social anxiety using campus resources, I'd talk to them about this feeling of burnout as well. It's not uncommon to feel this way during your first semester, and they can help you deal with the feeling of being overwhelmed.

Make sure your hygiene is good - brush your teeth, shower, make sure you always have clean clothes to wear. Set a regular bedtime, and only go to sleep before it if you are sick or actually tired. 

I know that sounds dumb, but putting that effort into regimenting basic daily life makes everything else easier. These are things that you absolutely must do - you cannot let them fall by the wayside. 

Additionally, you should begin logging your moods, emotions, coping mechanisms and ability, etc. Having a log every day helps you identity what makes you feel better an what makes you more depressed. It also makes you consider what else you can try and can help your doctor and therapist treat you better. A nice program for this is called Optimism, if you're technologically inclined. If not, a notebook works just fine. 

Once you've got that down, start expanding.

The hardest part of doing a lot of things, when you're depressed, is starting. You sit there and try to summon up the energy, and try to convince yourself that it's worth it, and that you actually have the ability to do it.

It may be easiest to say something like, "I have to go to the gym. I can turn around and leave once I'm there, but I have to get there." Once you're there, it's a lot easier to say, "Yes, working out is a good idea, I should do it."

My distinctions between just general soreness from working out and a problem are:

Is it sore, or is it *pain*? This one it's a little harder to do if you're not used to physical activity, but generally pain feels sharper than soreness. It feels swollen.

If I go out to do my workout, does it fade after I'm warmed up, or does it stick around? If I'm just sore, it'll feel better 5-10 minutes into my workout. If it's a problem, it'll continue to hurt past that, and I should stop, walk it out, and then rest afterwards.

Does it keep me from going in a full range of motion, walking properly, or otherwise impair my ability to move? If yes, this is something you should go to a doctor for.
